section.title: Doxology
section.sectionRationale: The letter closes as it opened, with the keeping power of God. After warning of fierce dangers, Jude lifts his readers' eyes to the One who is able to keep them from stumbling and to present them faultless before His glory. This burst of praise is the resolution of everything the letter has said.
section.thesis: The whole fight for the faith rests on the God who alone is able to keep His people from stumbling and to present them blameless with great joy; to Him, our only Savior through Jesus Christ, belongs all glory forever.
section.frameNote: One movement in two beats: the promise of God's keeping and presenting power, verse 24; and the ascription of glory to the only God our Savior through Jesus Christ, verse 25.

verses.text: Now to Him who is able to {{phylasso|keep}} you from {{aptaistos|stumbling}} and to present you {{amomos|unblemished}} in His glorious presence, with great joy,
to the {{monos|only}} God our Savior be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority through Jesus Christ our Lord before all time, and now, and for all eternity. Amen.

phylasso.gloss: To guard, protect, watch over as a sentinel guards what is entrusted to him. God is able to guard His people so that they do not fall away. It is the keeping theme of the whole letter, gathered now into a promise of His protecting power.

aptaistos.gloss: Without stumbling, sure-footed, not falling. The word pictures someone kept from tripping on a dangerous path. Amid the perils of false teaching, God is able to keep His own from the fatal stumble of apostasy and bring them safely through.

amomos.gloss: Blameless, without blemish, faultless. It was used of sacrificial animals fit for God. Believers will be presented not merely acquitted but spotless in His glorious presence, made faultless through Christ, the true unblemished Lamb.

monos.gloss: Only, alone, sole. Against the false teachers' distortions, Jude confesses the only God our Savior. There is one true God, and salvation belongs to Him alone, given through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom all glory is due.

basic.context: Jude ends with soaring praise. After all the warnings, he points to the One who can actually keep believers safe: God is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you faultless before His glory, and to do it with great joy. Then he gives God every honor, glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, through Jesus Christ, forever. It is the confident, worshipful close to a letter full of danger.
basic.hermeneutics: A doxology is not an add on; it is the point everything has been building toward. Jude has commanded believers to keep themselves, verse 21, and now assures them that God is the one able to keep them, verse 24. Human responsibility rests on divine power. The letter that began with kept in Jesus Christ ends with the God who keeps us from stumbling.
basic.originalLanguages: God is able to phylasso, guard, His people and keep them aptaistos, without stumbling, and to present them amomos, faultless, before His glory. Jude ascribes all glory to the monos, the only, God our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, before all time and forever.
basic.typology: To be presented amomos, unblemished, uses the language of the spotless sacrifice. What the Old Testament required of the offering, God Himself provides for His people in Christ, presenting them faultless, clothed in the perfection of the true unblemished Lamb.
basic.christ: The keeping and presenting are God's, and they come through Jesus Christ our Lord. He is the mediator through whom glory is given to God, and by whom sinners are made faultless. The letter that warned of those who deny our only Master ends by exalting Him as the Lord through whom the only God saves.
basic.god: God is able, He is our Savior, and He is the only God. He does not keep His people grudgingly but presents them with great joy. The whole letter's fearful warnings give way to this: the last word is not the danger of falling but the power and gladness of the God who holds His own.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 16 and other letters close with similar doxologies. First Thessalonians 5 promises that the faithful God will keep believers blameless. And Ephesians 5 speaks of Christ presenting the church without spot or blemish.
basic.oneStory: From the first promise in Eden to the last vision of the redeemed, the Bible tells of a God determined to bring a people safely home. Jude's doxology voices that assurance: the only God our Savior, through Jesus Christ, is able to keep us from stumbling and present us faultless in His presence with great joy, and to Him belongs glory forever.

context.literary:
These two verses are the last sentence of a short, fierce letter, and they are one long sentence in the Greek, built as a single sweep of praise. It opens with a relative pattern, 'to Him who is able', states two things He is able to do, and then runs through five nouns of honor and three time phrases before the closing Amen. The letter's shape makes the placement matter. Jude greets his readers in verses 1 and 2, explains in verses 3 and 4 why he changed his plan and wrote a warning instead of a treatise on salvation, and then spends verses 5 to 16 piling up examples of judgment: the generation brought out of Egypt, the angels who left their post, Sodom and Gomorrah, Cain, Balaam and Korah. Verses 17 to 19 turn to memory, 'remember what was foretold by the apostles', and verses 20 to 23 give four commands to the faithful. Only then does the tone change.

The change is prepared by a thread of repetition. Jude opened by calling his readers 'kept in Jesus Christ', verse 1. He then showed that those who fall are also 'kept', but in chains and in blackest darkness, verses 6 and 13. In verse 21 he tells believers to keep themselves in the love of God. Verse 24 is where the circle closes, with God as the one who guards. The same Greek family of ideas runs from the first line to the last, and the doxology is the point at which the keeping stops being a duty and becomes a promise.

The doxology also answers the letter's one great fear. Verses 4 to 19 are about people who slip in unnoticed and about believers who might be dragged away. A letter that ended on verse 23 would end on a task. Ending on verse 25 leaves the reader looking up.
context.historical:
Jude calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James, verse 1, which most readers take to mean a brother of the Lord's own family, since the James of the early church was well known and needed no other introduction, Acts 15:13 and Galatians 1:19. The letter shows no sign of a precise date or a named city. It was written to believers who knew the apostles' teaching, verse 17, and who were threatened by teachers who treated grace as permission for immorality, verse 4. It shares so much of its material with 2 Peter 2 that the two letters clearly belong to the same stream of early warning, whichever drew on the other.

The first hearers would have caught the weight of the closing words because letters in the Greek world normally ended with a short wish for health or a farewell. Jude, like Paul, replaces the farewell with a hymn. Doxologies of this kind grew out of Jewish prayer, where a blessing of God marked the end of a psalm book, Psalm 41:13 and Psalm 72:19, and where the congregation answered with Amen. A letter read aloud in a gathering would end with the listeners saying that Amen themselves.

The phrases 'to Him who is able' also had a settled home in apostolic worship. Paul closes Romans with 'Now to Him who is able to strengthen you', Romans 16:25, and Ephesians 3:20 begins a doxology the same way. Jude is writing in a tradition his readers already knew by ear. What would have struck them was the setting: a congregation under pressure from smooth, persuasive teachers, hearing that the gospel's keeping power was greater than the pressure.
context.canonical:
Jude's doxology belongs to a family of New Testament closings that begin with a statement of divine ability. Paul writes that the Lord 'is able to make him stand', Romans 14:4, and speaks of the God who 'is able to strengthen you', Romans 16:25. He commits the Ephesian elders to the word of grace 'which can build you up', Acts 20:32, and confesses that he is convinced Christ 'is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him for that day', 2 Timothy 1:12. Hebrews adds that Christ 'is able to save completely those who draw near', Hebrews 7:25. Each time, the ability is placed in God and never in the believer's own grip.

The Old Testament lies behind the picture. 'He preserves our lives and keeps our feet from slipping', Psalm 66:9, and 'He will not allow your foot to slip; your Protector will not slumber', Psalm 121:3. Israel's exodus is remembered as a journey in which God led them so that 'they did not stumble', Isaiah 63:13, and the promised return is on 'a level path where they will not stumble', Jeremiah 31:9.

The picture of being presented before God also has deep roots. Paul says Christ will 'present her to Himself as a glorious church, without stain or wrinkle', Ephesians 5:27, and that God reconciled believers 'to present you holy, unblemished, and blameless in His presence', Colossians 1:22. Peter's closing words likewise point to 'the day of eternity', 2 Peter 3:18. Jude's last sentence gathers all of this into one prayer, and the New Testament letters echo its structure again and again.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Jude wanted his readers to finish the letter standing on rock rather than on their own effort. He has asked a great deal of them. They are to contend for the faith, verse 3, build themselves up, pray, keep themselves in God's love, and pull some people out of danger while treating others with careful mercy, verses 20 to 23. A reader who stopped there might conclude that everything depends on their vigilance, and Jude knows that conclusion would crush them or make them proud.

So he ends by moving the weight. The same God who is the object of the believer's keeping is the subject of the guarding. The warnings are real, and the ones who left the right way are real examples, but the readers are not left to out-walk the false teachers on their own legs. Jude also meant them to leave in worship, not in anxiety. By closing with praise rather than a final threat, he teaches them to treat the whole letter as a reason to adore the One who holds them.

There is a pastoral aim for the ones who are afraid. Anyone reading verses 5 to 19 honestly will wonder whether they could fall. Verse 24 answers by naming God's power and His joy, in that order, and the answer is meant to be believed.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The doxology describes what God is able to do and invites the reader to say Amen. It does not give a new command, and it should not be turned into a technique for staying safe. What carries forward is the shape of the response. Ability that belongs to God is meant to be met with praise, and the believer's best defense against the pull of corrupt teaching is to keep looking at the One who keeps.

This verse also does not cancel the commands that precede it. Reading 'to keep you from stumbling' as a promise that nothing will ever need watching would ignore verses 20 to 23, and treating the commands as the whole story would ignore verse 24. Jude places them side by side deliberately. The believer builds, prays, shows mercy and keeps watch, and does all of it as one carried by a faithful God.

Because the doxology is a prayer addressed to God, it is also an example to copy. Believers are not only told that God keeps them; they are shown how to say so aloud, with a closing 'Amen' that makes the congregation a partner in the praise. Reading these verses well means reading them with the voice as well as the eye.

debates.question: How do God's keeping and the believer's keeping fit together?

views.label: God keeps, and that includes perseverance
views.case: The letter opens with believers 'kept in Jesus Christ', verse 1, and closes with God able to keep them from stumbling, verse 24. Passages such as John 10:28 and Romans 8:38 and 39 say no one can snatch them away. On this reading the command in verse 21 is the means God uses: He keeps His people by moving them to keep themselves, as Philippians 2:12 and 13 describe, 'work out your salvation' because 'it is God who works in you'.

views.label: The warnings are real and the possibility of falling is real
views.case: Jude's examples, the people destroyed after the exodus, verse 5, the angels who left their post, verse 6, show that proximity to God does not guarantee safety. Hebrews 3:12 likewise warns of a heart of unbelief that turns away. On this view verse 24 is a promise made to those who are in Christ and hold to Him, and the warnings are addressed to anyone tempted to leave.

views.label: The warnings describe the false teachers, not true believers
views.case: Some read the examples as portraits of people who were never inwardly united to Christ, so that the fall of the unbelieving generation and of the intruders does not suggest that true believers fall. Verse 4 calls them 'ungodly ones' and verse 19 says they are 'devoid of the Spirit'.

debates.bearing: Jude holds both lines together and does not choose between them. He commands keeping in verse 21 and promises it in verse 24, so a reading that drops either half misses his point. Whatever view a reader takes of final perseverance, the practical result is the same: live watchfully, and rest only in God's ability.

debates.question: Whose joy is the 'great joy' of verse 24?

views.label: The joy of the believers
views.case: The phrase can describe the people presented, who stand in God's presence glad beyond measure. The Greek word for joy here is one of exultation, the same word used when the unborn John leaped at Mary's greeting, Luke 1:44. On this reading the day of presentation is a day of delight for those who arrive.

views.label: The joy of God
views.case: The phrase can also describe the presenter. Scripture speaks of the LORD who will 'rejoice over you with gladness', Zephaniah 3:17, and of the joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, Luke 15:7. Hebrews 12:2 says Christ endured the cross 'for the joy set before Him', a joy that includes bringing His people home.

views.label: Both, because the sentence does not choose
views.case: The Greek leaves the owner of the joy open, and it may be deliberate. The picture is of a shared gladness, a God who delights to give and a people who delight to receive.

debates.bearing: The ambiguity is a gift. Whether the joy is God's, ours, or both, the final scene is not grim relief at a narrow escape. It is delight, and Jude wants his readers to expect that.

study.originalLanguages:
The sentence begins with a participle, dynamenos, 'the one who is able', from dynamai, the verb for ability and power. It stands first and carries the weight. Paul uses the same form at the head of the doxology in Romans 16:25, and again in Ephesians 3:20, so the pattern is familiar. What Jude stresses is that the ability belongs to God and is large enough for the whole job.

The verb for 'keep' in verse 24 is not the verb Jude has used elsewhere. In verses 1, 6, 13 and 21 he uses tereo, which means to watch over, to hold in custody, to preserve. In verse 24 he switches to phylasso, to guard, a word of sentry duty. Paul uses it of what Christ is able to guard, 2 Timothy 1:12. The change in word adds the picture of a watchman who stands between the believer and every enemy. The believer 'keeps' in verse 21, but the One who guards is a different and greater figure.

'Stumbling' is aptaistos, a word found only here in the New Testament. It means 'not tripping', a picture of surefooted walking, and it fits the psalms that praise the God who does not let a foot slip, Psalm 66:9 and Psalm 121:3. The wording is a negative compound, and it says exactly what the believer cannot promise himself.

The phrase 'in His glorious presence' translates katenopion, 'in the sight of' or 'before the face of', with doxa, glory. It appears in Ephesians 1:4 and Colossians 1:22, where believers are to stand 'holy and blameless in His presence'. The joy is agalliasis, exultant gladness, the word of leaping and shouting rather than quiet contentment.

The second verse brings the closing ascription: doxa, glory, megalosyne, majesty, kratos, dominion, and exousia, authority. Megalosyne appears in Hebrews 1:3 and 8:1, of the 'Majesty' at God's right hand, and the cluster reminds the reader that the God who guards is the ruler of all. The phrase 'before all time, and now, and for all eternity' is literally 'before all the age, and now, and into all the ages'. Past, present, and future are covered, and the first of the three reaches back before creation, to the place where, as Ephesians 1:4 says, God chose a people 'before the foundation of the world'. The title 'Savior', soter, joins 'only God', as in 1 Timothy 1:17 and 2:3, a link Isaiah 43:11 makes in the singular voice of the LORD: 'there is no Savior but Me.'

typology.fulfillment: The law said, 'You must not present anything with a defect, because it will not be accepted on your behalf.' An offering had to be whole before it was brought near. In the doxology the direction reverses. God Himself presents His people unblemished, so the standard that no worshiper could meet is met by the One who provides. Peter names the ground: believers were redeemed 'with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot', 1 Peter 1:19, and Hebrews says He 'offered Himself unblemished to God', Hebrews 9:14. The type falls short because animals were examined and approved for a short time, while believers are made fit for His presence once and for all.

typology.type: The Lord who holds up the walker, Psalm 37:24
typology.fulfillment: The psalmist says, 'Though he falls, he will not be overwhelmed, for the LORD is holding his hand.' Israel's story kept returning to a God who steadies His people along the way, and Isaiah 63:13 looks back to the exodus and asks of God, 'who led them through the depths like a horse in the wilderness, so that they did not stumble?' Jude shows the fulfillment in the work of Christ, who 'is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them', Hebrews 7:25. The type falls short in that it describes protection along the road, while Jude's promise carries all the way into the presence of God.

typology.type: Presented before God as a bride, Ephesians 5:27
typology.fulfillment: Marriage in the Old Testament is a picture of God's covenant with His people, as in Jeremiah 2:2, where the LORD remembers 'your love as a bride'. In Ephesians, Christ gave Himself up for the church 'to present her to Himself as a glorious church, without stain or wrinkle or any such blemish, but holy and blameless'. Jude's word 'present' belongs to the same picture, with the bridegroom as the one who makes ready. The type is incomplete in that an earthly bride can only be dressed by another, while the church is both loved and actually made holy by the One she is brought to meet.

study.christ:
Jude's last sentence has Christ at its edge and at its center. It closes with 'through Jesus Christ our Lord', verse 25, but it is Christ's work that makes verse 24 possible. The One who keeps is the one who has already done the keeping. He told the Father in the prayer of John 17 that while He was with His own He had 'protected and preserved them', John 17:12, and He wants them with Him 'where I am, that they may see the glory You gave Me', John 17:24. Jude's doxology is that prayer answered at the last.

The words 'through Jesus Christ' also place Him as the way by which worship reaches God. Christians do not praise God in some other name beside His. Peter speaks the same way, 'that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ', 1 Peter 4:11, and Paul closes Romans 'to the only wise God be glory forever through Jesus Christ', Romans 16:27. The mediator of salvation is also the mediator of praise.

The two verses also hold together the glory of Christ and His gentleness. Jude's first readers had heard of teachers who 'deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ', verse 4. The reply is to exalt Him, and to show that His authority is the same authority that guards His people. He has the power to keep because He holds the dominion, and He keeps because He is the Savior who loves.

The ground for presenting people blameless is His death. Paul says God reconciled believers 'by Christ's physical body through death to present you holy, unblemished, and blameless', Colossians 1:22. The believer can stand unblemished only because the Lamb was. Hebrews adds that He 'always lives to intercede', Hebrews 7:25, so the keeping has a living advocate, not just a past event.

A warning keeps the reading careful. The passage does not itself say that the guarding is Christ's alone, and the Father is the primary object of praise. The link to Christ is explicit in the words 'through Jesus Christ our Lord' and in the wider New Testament witness.
study.god:
The doxology shows God as able, and it names the ability before it names anything else. The One whom Jude praises is not a God who tries to keep His people and hopes for the best. He is the One who actually can, and the whole of Scripture supports the claim. The psalmist says the LORD 'will not allow your foot to slip; your Protector will not slumber', Psalm 121:3, and Moses says of Him, 'The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms', Deuteronomy 33:27.

The doxology shows God as one. Jude names Him the 'only God', and Scripture builds that claim into the title 'Savior': 'there is no Savior but Me', Isaiah 43:11, and again Hosea 13:4. If there were another savior, there would be another place to look when stumbling. The word 'only' therefore guards the believer as well as God's honor.

It shows God's joy. He presents His people 'with great joy', and the Bible does not describe a reluctant rescuer. 'He will rejoice over you with gladness,' says Zephaniah 3:17, and Jesus says heaven rejoices over each sinner who repents, Luke 15:7. A God who has to be talked into mercy could not close a letter like this.

It shows God as holy, because the aim is a people 'unblemished' in His 'glorious presence'. Nothing impure stands before Him. He does not lower the standard to fit the sinner; He lifts the sinner to the standard. And it shows Him as sovereign over time, as the title 'before all time, and now, and for all eternity' reaches from before creation to the age to come. That is where Ephesians 1:4 begins, 'He chose us in Him before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless in His presence'.

For worship, the sentence teaches that praise is the right response to a promise as well as to a deed. The glory, majesty, dominion and authority that Jude lists are what 1 Chronicles 29:11 offers, 'Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the splendor and the majesty'. Believers who feel fragile should say the words out loud, because they are meant to be said by weak people to a strong God.

crossReferences.note: Paul's own closing doxology opens with the same words, 'Now to Him who is able', and ends 'to the only wise God be glory forever through Jesus Christ'. The pattern shows that Jude is using a shape his readers already sang, and that the 'through Jesus Christ' ending was common apostolic practice.

Another doxology that begins with God's ability, 'to do so much more than all we ask or imagine'. Where Jude's emphasis falls on keeping, Paul's falls on giving beyond what we ask. Together they show a God whose power exceeds both our fears and our requests.

Paul prays that the God of peace will keep believers 'blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ', and adds, 'The One who calls you is faithful, and He will do it.' The ground of the promise is God's faithfulness, which is also the ground of Jude's confidence.

Christ 'gave Himself up for her' so that He might 'present her to Himself as a glorious church'. This is the closest parallel to Jude's idea of being presented. It makes plain that the presentation is the climax of a love already shown on the cross.

God reconciled believers 'by Christ's physical body through death to present you holy, unblemished, and blameless in His presence'. The vocabulary of presenting and blamelessness matches Jude's, and Paul supplies the cost behind the promise.

Paul is not ashamed because 'He is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him for that day'. The same ability and the same verb of guarding appear, and Paul shows what it looks like in a prison cell, where confidence in God's keeping outlasted every loss.

Jesus prays that the Father would protect His own, and says that while He was with them He 'protected and preserved them'. The Savior's prayer before the cross is the foundation for the doxology after the apostles.
'He will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand.' The 'able' language is used here of a believer's daily standing, and Jude carries it to the final standing before God's glory.

Believers 'through faith are shielded by God's power for the salvation that is ready to be revealed in the last time'. Peter links God's power, human faith and a future salvation in a single sentence, and shows the same balance Jude strikes.

Christ 'is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them'. The ability named by Jude is exercised through a living Priest, so the keeping is ongoing.

The letter opens with believers 'kept in Jesus Christ'. The doxology completes the frame: what was said at the start about their position is shown at the end as God's power. The beginning and the end say the same thing.

Believers are to build themselves up, pray in the Spirit, and 'keep yourselves in the love of God'. Verse 24 answers these commands directly, by saying who finally does the keeping. The commands and the promise are two halves of one picture.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with a world declared good and a people who stumbled out of it. Adam and Eve were driven from the garden, and the long history that followed is a record of unsteady feet: Israel at the Red Sea and then in the wilderness, kings who fell, and a people sent into exile. Against that background, the question of whether anyone can be kept all the way home is the central question of redemption.

Scripture answers by pointing to God's ability from its earliest pages. The patriarchs lean on a God who goes with them. The psalmists confess that their feet had almost slipped and that the LORD held them, Psalm 73:2. The prophets promise a road where they will not stumble, Jeremiah 31:9. What the Old Testament longs for, the New Testament announces as done in Christ, who 'always lives to intercede', Hebrews 7:25, and who will lose none of those the Father gave Him, John 6:39.

Jude's doxology takes its place near the end of that story as a final assurance written to a church that was under pressure. It tells believers living in the last times, verse 18, that the God who began the work will finish it. The same promise reappears in Philippians 1:6, where the One who began a good work 'will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus'.

The doxology also points forward to the new creation. The picture of people presented in the presence of God's glory is the picture of Revelation 22:4, where they 'will see His face'. Believers do not arrive on their own, nor do they arrive grimly. They arrive with joy, because the God who guarded them has been looking forward to the day, and when they do, the praise that Jude begins in two verses will be sung in full, 'Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanks and honor and power and strength be to our God forever and ever! Amen', Revelation 7:12.

sermon.title: Now to Him
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in Jude, this closing message expounds the doxology of Jude 1:24-25, praising the God who is able to keep His people from stumbling and present them faultless, and how that knowledge shapes worship and mission. A clear, orthodox handling of this movement.

quiz.q: What is the great assurance of verse 24?

options.text: God is able to keep believers from stumbling and to present them faultless before His glory.
options.note: Jude 1:24 places the believer's security in God's keeping and presenting power.

options.text: Believers must keep themselves faultless by their own strength.
options.note: The keeping here is God's ability, not our unaided effort.

options.text: God will present only the most successful believers.
options.note: The promise is for His people, kept by His power, not by their success.

options.text: Stumbling is inevitable and final for everyone.
options.note: The point is the opposite: God is able to keep His own from the fatal fall.

quiz.q: How does the doxology relate to the earlier command to keep yourselves, verse 21?

options.text: God's ability to keep us grounds and secures our own keeping.
options.note: Our perseverance rests on His preserving power, as in Philippians 1:6.

options.text: It cancels the command, so effort no longer matters.
options.note: It grounds the command rather than cancelling it; we keep ourselves because He keeps us.

options.text: It contradicts the command outright.
options.note: There is no contradiction; divine keeping and human keeping work together.

options.text: It means our keeping earns God's keeping.
options.note: His keeping is the ground of ours, not a reward we earn.

quiz.q: What does it mean that God will present believers unblemished?

options.text: Faultless and spotless, using sacrificial language, made perfect through Christ.
options.note: Amomos was used of unblemished offerings; believers are presented spotless in Christ.

options.text: Merely let off without any real transformation.
options.note: It is more than acquittal; they are made truly faultless in His presence.

options.text: Presented only if they never sinned at all.
options.note: It is God's doing through Christ, not a reward for a sinless record.

options.text: Left in their sin but overlooked by God.
options.note: They are made blameless, not merely overlooked.

quiz.q: How does Jude describe God as he gives Him glory in verse 25?

options.text: The only God our Savior, glorified through Jesus Christ our Lord forever.
options.note: Jude 1:25 confesses the one God as Savior, honored through Christ for all eternity.

options.text: One of many gods worthy of some honor.
options.note: Jude confesses the only God, guarding true monotheism.

options.text: A distant God who takes no part in salvation.
options.note: He is expressly our Savior, deeply involved in saving His people.

options.text: A Savior apart from any role for Jesus Christ.
options.note: Glory is given through Jesus Christ our Lord; the Son is central.

quiz.q: What tone does God's keeping carry at the end of the letter?

options.text: Great joy: God delights to present His people faultless before His glory.
options.note: Jude 1:24 says with great joy, ending the letter on gladness, not dread.

options.text: Reluctant duty on God's part.
options.note: The text says great joy, not reluctance.

options.text: Cold indifference toward the outcome.
options.note: Far from indifferent, God rejoices to keep and present His own.

options.text: Anxious uncertainty about whether He can succeed.
options.note: He is able, and He acts with joy; there is no uncertainty.

questions: The letter warned of many dangers, then ended by saying God is able to keep you from stumbling. How does that promise steady you when you feel your own weakness?
You are told both to keep yourselves and that God keeps you. How does trusting His power change the way you pursue perseverance?
God will present His people faultless, and He does it with great joy. How does it move you to know that God delights, not merely consents, to save you?
Jude gives God every honor, glory, majesty, dominion, and authority. What would it look like for your daily life to give God that place in practice?
The letter ends in worship after facing real threats. How can praise become your own response to danger and uncertainty, rather than only fear?

translationNotes.note: Keep you from stumbling renders phylasso with aptaistos, guarded so as not to fall.

Some manuscripts add through Jesus Christ our Lord and the fuller list of attributes; the BSB reflects the best attested text. Before all time, and now, and for all eternity renders a sweeping expression of God's everlasting glory.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Jude 1:24-25.
